# Overview

MiSA identifies disease-associated spatial dysbiosis by testing whether the spatial organization of microbial taxa differs between clinical groups, using image-based microbiome data. A typical analysis follows these steps:

1. **Preprocessing:** identify the region of study (i.e., the area colonized by microbes) in each image and build observation windows (`kde_est()`, `alpha_windows()`).
2. **Taxon-level testing:** characterize the spatial distribution of each
   taxon with the summary function *d(r)* and compare it between groups using
   the four MiSA variants.
3. **Community-level testing:** combine the taxon-level results to assess
   overall spatial dysbiosis.

Step 1 is described in the *Preprocessing* section, and steps 2 and 3 in *MiSA test* section. 

Step 1 is optional. Users who already have observation windows for their images can pass them directly to `estimate_L()` when running MiSA. If step 1 is skipped entirely, `estimate_L()` uses a default window: the convex hull of the cell locations.

The following packages are required for functions and examples in the MiSA package: ggplot2, grid, harmonicmeanp, spatstat.explore, spatstat.geom, stats, deldir, sf.

```{r setup}
library(MiSA)
```

# Preprocessing

In this step, we determine the true region of study (i.e., the area colonized by microbes) in each image. We first estimate the density of cells across the image, then build observation windows around the high-density regions.

## Visialuze the example data

The example image is stored as a data frame with columns `x` and `y` (the spatial coordinates of each cell) and `taxon_name` (the taxon identity of each cell).

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
data(example_image)
plot_centroid(example_image)
```

## Kernel density estimate of cell locations

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
img_kde <- kde_est(example_image)

# visualize the distribution of density
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(img_kde, main="Kernel Density Estimation")
hist(img_kde$v, main = "Distribution of estimated density", xlab = "density")
abline(v=0.002, lty=2)
```

## Determine region of study 

`alpha_windows()` builds observation windows around the high-density cell
regions in each image. Separated regions are kept apart, and each is returned
as its own `owin` object, sorted by area from largest to smallest.

`alpha` controls how tightly the window follows the shape of the high-density
region, in the same units as the coordinates. Smaller values give a tighter,
more detailed boundary, and larger values give a smoother one. The default is
200.

We set `cutoff = 0.002` based on the histogram of estimated densities. Areas
with a kernel density below 0.002 are excluded from further analysis.

With `fill_holes = TRUE`, holes within each region are filled, so each window
is bounded by its outer boundary only.

```{r}
wins <- alpha_windows(img_kde, alpha = 200, cutoff = 0.002, fill_holes = TRUE)
```

`plot_regions()` draws all observation window regions on a single plot, labeled
by name. It also returns the union of all regions as a single window (an owin object), which we save as `W_all`.

Because each separated region is returned as its own window, users can use a
single region or combine several (e.g., `W <- spatstat.geom::union.owin(wins$region1, wins$region2)`) as the true region of study.

In this example, we use `region1`, the largest region, as the region of study and plot it over the example image. 

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
W_all <- plot_regions(wins)

W <- wins$region1
plot(example_image$x, example_image$y, pch=20, col="pink", cex=0.1, main = "Microbial map with study region (window W)", xlab = "", ylab = "")
plot(W, add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
```

When running MiSA, `W` can be used as the window for this image by including it in the `groupA_window_list` or `groupB_window_list` argument of `estimate_L()`. These arguments take a named list with one entry per image, where the names match the image IDs, e.g. `groupA_window_list <- list("image1" = W, "image2" = NULL, "image3" = NULL, ...)`. Images set to `NULL` use the default window (the convex hull of the cell locations).

# MiSA test

## Sample Data

We demonstrate MiSA using the sample data included in the package, which were simulated based on real oral biofilm imaging data. We need imaging data for both the health and disease groups, each provided as a named list of data frames, with each data frame representing one image. Ensure every image in the list has a name assigned to it.

```{r}
data(diseaseImg.list)             
data(healthImg.list)

names(healthImg.list)
```

Each image data frame must contain columns named "x", "y", and "taxon_name", representing the x and y spatial coordinates and the corresponding taxon identity. We then visualize two images from the sample data, one from the health group and one from the disease group, by plotting the centroid of each microbial cell.

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
str(healthImg.list[['image1']])
str(diseaseImg.list[['image1']])

plot_centroid(healthImg.list[['image1']])
plot_centroid(diseaseImg.list[['image1']])
```

## Estimate Spatial Summary Function

### Estimate L Curves

To estimate the $L$ curves, we first pass the two lists containing our sample imaging data, `healthImg.list` and `diseaseImg.list` to `groupA_image_list` and `groupB_image_list`, respectively. 

A sequence of radii, `r_all`, must be pre-specified, over which the $L$ function will be evaluated. This set of radii will be used consistently across all images and must be carefully determined based on the spatial range of images.
In this example, we pre-specified the sequence of radii as  $r=0, 6, 12, \dots, 1500$, with a step size of 6. The maximum radius, `rmax`, was set to 1500, which is $0.375 \times 4000$, with 4000 being the side length of the square image. In general, it is recommended to set the maximum $r$ no larger than 0.5 times the length of the shortest side of the enclosing study region, to account for the border effect.

`taxa_all` contains all taxa of interest.

Users can provide a pre-defined study region for the images in `groupA` or `groupB` by passing input to `groupA_window_list` or `groupB_window_list`. The input should be a named list for the corresponding group, with each element being an object of class `owin` (short for "observation window"), as required by the `window` argument of `spatstat.geom::ppp()`. If a window is provided, its name must match the corresponding image's name in `groupA_image_list` or `groupB_image_list`. Users can specify a window (study region) for some images and leave others as `NULL`. If `NULL` is provided (either for a single image or the entire list), the function will go with the default setting and derive a convex hull from the data.

`border_correct` can be chosen from `"border"`, `"iso"`, and `"trans"`. For spatial microbiome data, it is always recommended to select `"border"`, as the other two options will substantially increase computation time.

```{r}
rmax  = 1500
r_all <- seq(0, rmax, length.out = 251) 
taxa_all <- unique(healthImg.list[[1]]$taxon_name)

L_result <- estimate_L(groupA_image_list=healthImg.list, groupB_image_list=diseaseImg.list, 
                    taxa=taxa_all, r_vec=r_all,
                    groupA_window_list = NULL, groupB_window_list = NULL,
                    border_correct = "border")
```

### Estimate d Curves

`estimate_d` takes the estimated $L$ curves for `groupA` and `groupB` as input, and outputs the estimated $d$ curve and the group label (`groupA` or `groupB`) for each image.

```{r}
d_result <- estimate_d(groupA_L = L_result$groupA_L, groupB_L = L_result$groupB_L, taxa = taxa_all,r_vec = r_all)
```

Visualize $d$ curves for each individual taxon, colored by groups.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(2,5))
for (taxon in taxa_all){
  d.mat <- d_result[[taxon]]
  r <- as.numeric(colnames(d.mat$d))
  matplot(r, t(d.mat$d), type = "l", lty = 1, col = ifelse(d.mat$group =="groupB", "red","black"), main=taxon, ylab = "d", xlab="r")
}
```

## Data Preparation for MiSA Test

The `MiSA_data` function prepares $d$ curves for MiSA test. Within each taxon, it first filters out images with limited spatial range, i.e., images whose $d$ curve does not have valid values up to a radius threshold, `r_thresh`. By default (`r_thresh = NULL`), $d$ curves that do not reach $0.5 \times$ `max(r_all)` will be excluded. Users may set `r_thresh` based on the scientific question of interest; for example, `r_thresh = 500` will exclude $d$ curves that do not have valid estimates up to $r=500$. For the curves that are kept, the function truncates the estimated $d$ curves to the maximum $r$ shared in common across all images (in both groups) for that taxon.

```{r}
data_pre <- MiSA_data(est_d = d_result, r_thresh = NULL)
```

`MiSA_check` drops taxa that are not valid for hypothesis testing via MiSA, based on the following criteria:

1. Only one group remains after filtering.

2. The total sample size is $\leq 2$.

3. $d$ has one or fewer valid estimates.

```{r}
data_checked <- MiSA_check(data_list = data_pre)
```

Use the following code to visualize the $d$ curves prepared for hypothesis testing.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(2,5))
for (taxon in taxa_all){
  d.mat <- data_checked[[taxon]]
  r <- as.numeric(colnames(d.mat$d))
  matplot(r, t(d.mat$d), type = "l", lty = 1, col = ifelse(d.mat$group =="groupB", "red","black"), main=taxon, ylab = "d", xlab="r")
}
```

## Identify Spatial Dysbiosis via MiSA

### MiSA-area

MiSA-area produces taxon-specific $p$-values and effect sizes. This function uses whichever group is entered as `groupA` as the reference group. In our case, the reference group is Health. A negative effect size indicates that the summary statistic ($d_\text{area}$) is smaller in the reference group (Health) than in the comparison group (`groupB`: Disease), and hence reflects a smaller deviation from CSR for Health compared to Disease. This indicates that the Disease group is more spatially structured, exhibiting stronger spatial patterns (e.g., clustering, patches, etc.) in the microbiome context.

A community-level $p$-value is also obtained to assess dysbiosis.

```{r}
results_area <- MiSA(misa_data_list = data_checked, method = "area")
results_area
```

### MiSA-sup

Similar to MiSA-area, MiSA-sup produces taxon-specific $p$-values and effect sizes by comparing summary statistic $d_\text{sup}$ between the two groups. 

```{r}
results_sup <- MiSA(misa_data_list = data_checked, method = "sup")
results_sup
```

### MiSA-orig

For the MiSA-orig method, users may want to select radii of interest and then obtain a combined $p$-value across the individual tests performed at those radii. To do this, you can either pick specific radii using `omnibus_r`, e.g., `omnibus_r = c(300, 600, 900)`. This will compare the original statistic $d$ at $r=300,600,900$ (consistently used across all taxa) and combine the individual $p$-values via HMP.

Alternatively, you may use `omnibus_num` to specify the number of radii you would like to test, e.g., `omnibus_num = 6` will test 6 radii evenly spaced across the full range of radii available in `misa_data_list`. Note that the resulting radii may vary across taxa, since different taxa may have different spatial ranges.

If `omnibus_r` is specified, the function will always use `omnibus_r`, regardless of the input for `omnibus_num`. If `omnibus_r` is left at its default (`NULL`) and `omnibus_num` is specified, the function will use `omnibus_num` instead. If both `omnibus_r` and `omnibus_num` are defaults (`NULL`), the function will set `omnibus_num = min(5, c-1)`, where `c` is the number of radii available for that taxon.

```{r}
results_orig <- MiSA(misa_data_list = data_checked, method = "orig", omnibus_r = NULL, omnibus_num = NULL)
# results_orig <- MiSA(MiSA_data = MiSA_data_list, method = "orig", omnibus_r = c(300, 600, 900))
# results_orig <- MiSA(MiSA_data = MiSA_data_list, method = "orig", omnibus_num = 6)

results_orig[c("taxon_results", "community_pval")]
```

Extract the $p$-values per radius.

```{r}
results_orig[["per_r_pval"]]
```

### MiSA-abs

Similar to MiSA-orig, MiSA-abs compares the absolute value of the statistic $d$ over the selected radii instead.

```{r}
results_abs <- MiSA(misa_data_list = data_checked, method = "abs")
results_abs[c("taxon_results", "community_pval")]
```

Extract the $p$-values per radius.

```{r}
results_abs[["per_r_pval"]]
```
